utterances.text: We gave you a videotape of the locality -- that is, the video that we saw in court today -- and we see a white board on a pole in the woods. What were you able to conclude from that videotape?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: I viewed that tape in detail, and I drew from it what I consider to be relevant facts which might be of significance. The videotape shows the place where the body was found, according to the experts there, and the relationship between that spot and Vlatko Kupreskic's house and the Busovaca/Vitez road. Having viewed the videotape, one can conclude that the position was established where the Prosecution witness saw the dead body of Fata Pezer (redacted)

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, where the victims were found. And he marked those places with a board, 50 by 50 centimetres, on a 4-metre-high pole. On the basis of the viewing of that tape, because my analysis was based exclusively on that video, I looked in the direction north/north-west, towards Vlatko Kupreskic's house, and the house is not visible. There is no optical visibility. On the recording itself one can see that on the left there is a steep slope. It is impossible to say how steep it is from the recording, but it is a slope. Behind it is a broad-leaved wood and brush wood. Of course, the filming was not done at the time of the event, so it is difficult to talk about the vegetation; but in any event, it was between four and five metres high, which is also confirmed by the testimony of the second witness, who, at one point in time, says that the wood was the height of a stodzina (sic), and the stodzina is the pole used in the middle of a haystack. So that would be four to five metres high, and that was the comparison he made to describe the height of the trees in the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, from this videotape, you were able to see the directions from which that position can be seen, the possible position of the wounding, and also you were able to see the configuration of the land, the woods, of course, as they are now. Is there anything else which you used from that tape?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that tape, one comes to the conclusion that from the position where the victims were marked to have been, there is no optical visibility towards Vlatko Kupreskic's house, and vice versa; there is no visibility between Vlatko Kupreskic's house and those spots. As the shots were taken from various sides, various positions, the view from Donji Ahmici, the Vitez side of the main road, towards the north, one can easily see the board. It is also visible from the direction of the school in Donji Ahmici. That is the road opposite to the position marked, but to the south, southwards, and to the south-west from those places, that point can be seen, the point where the victim is marked to have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us also add, where there is optical visibility, that is where the infantry weapons may be used?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Any kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Right. You also saw a video recording where the witness shows where he was wounded and how he was wounded; you know the tape. The witness describes the event, tells us how he did perceive that particular moment when he was fired at, and what he noted at the time. Could you tell us whether that tape was of any use to you, and what conclusions did you draw from that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that videotape, on our finding and our written analysis, it was really of major importance, because this witness gave us his version of the dynamics which the events followed, how he moved, how that large group moved from the Pezers' or whoever's house, and the direction in which they were moving. And from that tape, I took out -- and I'm quoting, as a matter of fact, the words that he said during the recording. He said that there were about 15 of them who set off across the meadow, across the clearing, towards the wood, and at first they had high hornbeam, and then they had thicker brush wood, something like that. When they were coming to the middle of the wood, then there were shots fired at them from the back. So we saw on the film Vlatko Kupreskic's house, which is beyond the hill, where we have a proper woods in the middle, and at that moment, Vlatko Kupreskic's house is to the left and behind, and there is no optical visibility between these two places. Now, when the group is in the middle of this proper woods, they dispersed. They didn't go in a single file; they spread out over a line of some five or six metres between them. At that moment the witness was wounded in the neck and in the area of his shoulder blade, and the woman, Fata, fell dead, and he says to the left of him. He said she never let out a sound. The girl, (redacted), who was to the right of him, was wounded in the right leg, and he said her whole right leg was torn apart. If that is to the left of him was a dead woman, he was in the middle, and the wounded girl was to his right-hand side, and it all happened over an area of some five or six metres long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what does this distribution mean to you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is very important in view of the injuries they sustained, and I'll come to that, but let me finish with this, what I saw on the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Do go on.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as for the weapon that was fired from, this witness believes it was an 84; that is, the machine gun. That is, in brackets, he says 84, but he doesn't say it is a machine gun, but this is a machine gun. 7,62 times 54R, I believe that, but he says it was not an automatic weapon, it was a more powerful weapon, because it must have been fragmentation ammunition, and he knows it because leaves were burning, and the leaves were cut off the branches as if by a saw, and that he saw branches falling -- he is showing with his thumb or something, and he says the branches could have been four or five centimetres thick, and yet they were cut off as if sawn off. That is what I saw on that film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let us go back to the medical documentation that was admitted, both for -- equally for (redacted). What could you conclude from this documentation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since we were together with medical forensic experts, we have a complete finding; that is, we had a forensic expert, and I also went through that and noted that the witness sustained injury on the right side of his neck. It was interpreted then by Dr. Skavic. He said that it went through, it was a tangential wound on the neck passing through a groove, through a channel -- I don't know how long it is -- and then the exit wound is above the right shoulder blade. We looked at the direction of the channel, which very markedly goes from above downwards. It goes -- it is a descending channel, and from the front to the back. I believe you asked the doctor about that. As for (redacted), one can see that she sustained severe injuries both in her upper and lower leg, except that it was again the right leg in her case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the basis of all that you analysed, you came to some conclusions, you came to some findings, which you told us about. Let us repeat them once again. You believe that the instrument in question was a heavy-calibre weapon. What could you tell us about the projectile? Was it a bullet, or a fragmentation bullet, a shrapnel, or what?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: If the data available to me are true, and if the witness spoke the truth, and if the finding of the length there was authentic and veracious, if all that is true, then it must have been a fragmentation bullet, or rather a projectile, which hit the tree crowns. I think that was why the tree crowns were shattered, because if you have the optical visibility, when we say that we can see that marker post and the plate, which marked the position of the injured, from the road or the Busovaca/Vitez, Gornji Ahmici, and the school, and so on and so forth, even in that case, the injured persons wouldn't have been visible in the middle of the woods, but fire might have been opened at the woods from any direction; that is, from any place from which one could see the treetops. That is why I said that it was a fragmentation bullet. There are several factors indicating that. First, the nature of the injuries sustained. We have no information about the woman who died. We do not know from which direction she was hit, but one can say with certainty, with regard to the witness hit in the right neck -- and I'm talking about the direction either the projectile or the shrapnel, and to my mind, it is just a fragment -- I think these are fragments which flew all over the treetops. We see that it came -- that the direction was downward. The photograph, perhaps, is not completely authentic, but I did see the photograph, and after the surgical intervention -- and of course I do understand while the first aid was extended, at the time, nobody paid much attention to the aesthetics. But nevertheless, the channel, which is 6 centimetres long, is too irregular in shape to be due to poor surgery, so that it must have been due to a body of irregular shape. On the other hand, we have very severe injuries of the right upper leg and lower leg, and this could not have been done by a small-calibre bullet, so that one needs to exclude when a bullet hits the tree crown. It would be another matter if it were a direct hit, but it could have been caused by -- so that I think that the tree crowns must have been hit by a projectile of a sizeable calibre. I would say the lower threshold would be 7.62 times 54R, which is the machine gun MK-84. This is relatively a light bullet, and it couldn't cause such consequences. All the more so, it could not have caused it in April; the leaves only had just emerged from the tree, and so that of course, if they were incendiary bullets, they could have caused that injury. But as I said, the leaves were just beginning to bud, so that is why I believe that it was 12,7, 14,5, up to anti-aircraft gun of 20-millimetre calibre, because these bullets are much heavier, much more destructive. They carry also explosives, and when they hit an obstacle they simply burst; that is, the sleeve bursts, and then the fragments may cause the described injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in your practice -- there was this war, and you are well familiar with the situation, the types of weapons and injuries -- was it common, is that why this fragmentation ammunition was used, so that the targets in the woods or wherever are aimed at in that manner? I mean, that is, the target is not directly aimed at, but that the fire is opened on treetops or something like that, so that to have fragments ricocheting, or what?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I am referring to anti-aircraft machine gun or anti-aircraft gun, well, the name itself says that it is meant to bring aircraft down, but of course it was also used in ground combat. I can tell you that in the early days of the war, in '91, '92, when the first line was being put, and there was -- woods was there, and our combatants believed that they would be protected better if they dug their trenches in the woods. But when fire was opened on treetops, then very many of them died, killed by those fragments of these fragmentation bullets. Then they moved their defence lines, their trenches, in front of the woods, and then they were spared that kind of losses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything else in your findings that you believe of importance, and that you should tell us, that I missed to ask you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't really think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then. I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I should merely like to tender into evidence the analysis submitted by Professor Catipovic and Professor Skavic. Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I have only one question, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, from what -- first let me tell you that I'm lawyer Petar Pavkovic. From what you told us today, one could conclude that you have a very rich experience behind you; I believe I am right in saying that. So over all these years that you were involved in ballistics and in firearms and so on and so forth, you have had ample chance of seeing various firearms, hand-held firearms, and various other weapons. You will agree with me that if we take one criterion, and when it comes to hand-held firearms, we can define it as weapons from which one can open fire -- that fire at individuals, and also from which one can open bursts of fire. So that would be one criterion: One bullet at a time or bursts of fire. Secondly, I assume you had ample opportunity of familiarising yourself with a firearm called M-48.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is, can this rifle be used -- can one fire bursts of fire from that particular weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, you can only fire individual bullets. Every time, you have to pull the trigger, and by hand, you have to eject the empty cartridge from the barrel and then fire the next bullet. That is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Michael Blaxill; I am one of the prosecuting counsel assigned to this case. I do have just a few questions I would like to put to you as a result of what you have said. Just a little while ago, we heard from Professor Skavic that he felt that any analysis of medical documentation can only be carried out by properly qualified medical people. As a result, sir, is it correct to say that your comments on the injuries sustained by the two people are as a result of your collaboration in this task with Professor Skavic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: We cooperated very closely, and we co-signed our findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the final conclusion earlier this morning, Professor Skavic stated that he couldn't make a firm choice between bullet fragments or bullets from hand-held weapons as being the cause of the injury; either were possibilities. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do agree. I also say that without material evidence, one cannot affirm, really, anything. But if you have all the other circumstances and the material available to us, this sounds highly plausible to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you've hit the nail on the head for me, sir. The factual bases that you had to work with, if I understand correctly, were the medical documents that we've seen in court today, the videotape made by 16 (redacted), and the cross-section drawing of the land by the surveyor, Mr. Kesic. Am I correct in that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Only that, exclusively that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is exclusively your information?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding, for instance, one example, the fixing of the point called "F": Do you know what materials were provided to the surveyor, Mr. Kesic, to reach his conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this aerial photograph is mentioned there. The aerial photograph, and all the rest, he described in his finding, in writing, which was shown to me, and which was of use to us to see how he worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to put one other point to you, sir, and that is this: We have a point F, which is on one side of a hill, and if you remember the cross-section drawing of Mr. Kesic, we have the hill, then we have some lower ground, and then a house. Would you agree with me, from your recollection of that drawing, that there would be a clear line of sight from the house to the side of the hill that faced that house?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I were to say to you, theoretically, that people could have been on the side of that hill, they were shot at by a group of people near the house, and in fact the wounded or dead were dragged over the top to safety, now, if I give you that scenario, sir, would you now agree that hand-held firearms could have been used, bearing in mind direct line of sight in that circumstance and the -- let's say a distance of maybe under 100 metres? Would that now be possible, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: It would be possible, since there is a clear line of sight, to fire from the area of the house of the accused in the direction of the hill slope all the way up to the top of the hill, but -- yes, there is such a possibility; however, now the question arises as to the infliction of injuries; that is, the distribution of people who were there; that is, with which side of their bodies they were turned to. If both were hit to the right, on the right side, then they must have been turned with their right body to the house of Vlatko Kupreskic's, and that is not the direction in which they were running away from these houses. And secondly we hear this witness who was wounded in the neck. There we have the explicit direction, which is downward, very explicit, downward direction, and from the front to the back, so that he must have been -- he must have faced the house, actually, and very much bent, and looking in the direction of the barrel of the weapon from which the shot was fired, and that does not sound very logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, may I suggest to you this: We heard from Mr. Kesic this morning that he agreed that his cross-section drawing was essentially done by taking different height points from a map and then drawing straight lines between them to give a representation of relative elevations. If I remember correctly -- and no doubt I'll be corrected by others if I'm wrong -- he also said that, clearly, that the terrain between two such points can obviously undulate; it is not a straight line. Have you, sir, yourself, inspected the terrain between the house of Vlatko Kupreskic and the hill opposite?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not go out into the field. I have never been in Ahmici, and I used only what has already been mentioned and shown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, therefore, the relative positions or movements of individuals you have not heard from their own statements or testimony, because I understand --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing, no. Nor do I know anything more about it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question, if I may, sir, and that's this: Hand-held guns like machine guns, automatic rifles and the like, what sort of calibre ammunition do they tend to be? Can you give me an indication?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Listen, there are all sorts of calibres, but the most common is 7,62 and 39. These are the so-called automatic rifles which can be found the world over, if I may say so, and so the majority of automatic rifles would have the same calibre. It's accepted that 7,62 is mostly the Russian calibre, but you have the 30,08, and there are also bigger ones I just mentioned. But that is -- yes, there are much smaller, of course, but their bullets are faster, five, six centimetres (sic) or 5,45 millimetres and so forth, working on the same principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does a weapon like the AK-47, which is a fairly commonly-made weapon, is that a 7,62 calibre?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is 7,62 times 39.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe when you were discussing a few moments ago the kind of calibre of projectile that you thought was involved on the information you had received, I think you said the bottom threshold for that was indeed 7,63. Would you agree with that, sir? Did I hear you and understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: 7,62 times 54. It is slightly heavier than the one used by AK-47s but is the same calibre, 7,62. But the difference is in the weight of the bullets, because AK-47 bullets weigh eight grams with the sleeve and the nucleus, and the other one is 9,63 grams, and it is still very little, in view of the effect it has. But it still makes it possible as the lower threshold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any weapons which can taken, in fact, a variety of power of the same calibre bullet? In other words, a 7,62, can you fit two or three different powers of velocity of bullet in the same rifle, maybe at different times?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR CATIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the manufacturer and the ammunition itself, but it is somewhere within the same range. So in case of AK-47, it is about 740 metres per second. The velocity of others is about 800 metres or so. But in view of -- but their initial velocity is about the same. There are some faster, 900 or 1.000, but those are mostly smaller calibres. They also have a highly-destructive power but in case of human targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Thank you very much indeed. Your Honours, that concludes my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No, I do not have any additional questions, Your Honours. I'm only not sure whether D54/3 was admitted. That was the finding of the expert witnesses. I have no other questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, D54/3 was admitted into evidence, yes. Now, we still have half an hour. I wonder whether you have the fourth expert witness available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I will explain how we planned the production of further evidence. Tonight a factual witness is coming, and he will give his testimony tomorrow. We have no other witnesses for tomorrow. On Thursday at 9.00, Professor Wagenaar should come. He cannot change his schedule. So tomorrow we have only one witness, and on Thursday, in the morning at 9.00, another expert witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I should apologise to Mr. Catipovic, because I forgot that I should ask my colleagues if they have any questions. We don't have any questions for you, Mr. Catipovic. Thank you so much for coming to The Hague to testify in court. Thank you. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm released, I can go now? Right. Thank you, with pleasure. (The witness withdrew) (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par, I would like to ask you a question on behalf of the Court. Since you have one witness tomorrow and the last witness on Thursday, we are wondering whether you think that we can get through each in a matter of two hours, say by 11.00, so that Judge May may sit in another case, just to take advantage of the fact that we would be finishing pretty soon, pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I believe that examination-in-chief of the witness will not take more than 20 minutes or so. And as for the expert witness, I do not think that examination-in-chief will take more than 20 minutes or so. Of course, I do not know about the cross-examination, but I do not think that either of them should take more than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So therefore we may decide that we will be sitting tomorrow and on Thursday from 9.00 to 11.00, of course I mean subject to any further possibility of prolonged --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, definitely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
